senses: A complex structure, such as a society, considered as a single entity that contains numerous similar, smaller-scale structures.
The universe.
ety: From Middle French macrocosme (from Old French macrocosme) and Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “great, long”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”).

senses: Industrious; active.
Earnest; serious.
ety: From deed + -y. Cognate with Scots deedie, deedy (“active”). Compare also German tätig (“active”).

senses: Dressed in trousers.
ety: From trouser + -ed.

senses: That which makes something rustic.
ety: From rustic + -ity, from Latin rusticitas.

senses: A ragged, stunted tree or branch.
ety: Perhaps related to Norwegian skragg (a lean person), dialectal Swedish skragge (old and torn thing), Danish skrog (hull, carcass); perhaps related to shrink.

senses: The fat-tailed sheep.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi दुम्बा (dumbā), itself from दुम्बक (dumbaka, “thick-tailed sheep”).

senses: A drinking song in which each person is toasted.
ety: Borrowed from Italian brindisi.

senses: Being or having an intercalary day, particularly the quadrennial leap day of the Julian and Gregorian calendars traditionally placed as a "second sixth" day before March 1st.
ety: From Latin bisextilis/bissextilis (annus) (“bissextile year”), from bisextus + -ilis, from bis- (“two; twice; doubled”) + sextus (“sixth”) + dies (“day”), from the Julian calendar's original reckoning of its quadrennial intercalary day as a 48-hour February 24, subsequently distinguished as the two separate days of the sixth day before the March calends (ante diem sextum Kalendas Martias) and the "doubled sixth day". (February 24 is now normally understood as five days before the first of March, but was called the sixth by the Romans owing to their inclusive counting of dates. See Roman calend

senses: To frighten greatly; to fill with terror.
To menace or intimidate.
ety: From Middle French terrifier, from Latin terrificare.

senses: Made up of parts that are easily removable.
ety: From Ancient Greek κλαστός (klastós, “broken in pieces”), from κλάω (kláō, “to break”) + -ic.

senses: Someone who smiles.
ety: From Middle English smyler, smylere; equivalent to smile + -er.
examples: Jenny hadn’t been a natural hugger, but she’d been a smiler, a handholder.

senses: A type of boat used especially in the Hebrides and West Highlands of Scotland in the Middle Ages.
ety: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic bìrlinn, from Old Norse byrðingr.

senses: A waterspout.
ety: From New Latin prēstēr, from Ancient Greek πρηστήρ (prēstḗr, “hurricane or waterspout attended with lightning; (in plural) veins of the neck when swollen by anger”).

senses: A dish, of Swiss origin, similar to a fondue, consisting of melted cheese traditionally served on boiled potatoes and accompanied with pickles.
A firm cheese suitable for use in this dish.
ety: Borrowed from French raclette, the diminutive form of racler.

senses: To secrete vaginal lubrication from sexual arousal.
ety: Blend of girl + drool.

senses: The date on which a television or radio program is broadcast.
ety: From air + date.

senses: A tendency to talk excessively about oneself.
A belief that one is superior to or more important than others.
The result or product of being egoistic.
ety: From Latin ego (“I”) + -t- (perhaps modelled on dogmatism, despotism, idiotism) + -ism.

senses: To open something using a zipper.
To come open by means of a zipper.
ety: From un- + zip.
examples: He turned back and started unzipping a bag.

senses: Bituminous coal.
A type or grade of bituminous coal.
ety: From French bitumineux.

senses: The design and manufacture of biorobots
The study of biological "machines" (such as ribosomes)
ety: From bio- + robotics.

senses: An answer, especially a dismissal, or a woman's rejection of a marriage proposal.
Anything erected or planted as a symmetrical double.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani جَوَاب (javāb) / जवाब (javāb), from Classical Persian جَوَاب (jawāb), from Arabic جَوَاب (jawāb).

senses: Having macules; spotted
ety: From macula or macule + -ar.

senses: A synthetic plastic derived from cellulose.
ety: From cellulose + -ic.

senses: A mark ⟨ ‸ ⟩ used by writers and proofreaders to indicate that something is to be inserted at that point.
An exponentiation symbol or operator ⟨＾⟩.
An indicator, often a blinking line or bar and usually called a cursor, indicating where the next insertion or other edit will take place.
ety: From the Latin caret (“it lacks”), the third-person singular present active indicative form of careō (“to lack”).

senses: Exhibiting dichroism.
Exhibiting dichromatism; dichromatic.
ety: from Ancient Greek δίχρως (díkhrōs, “two-coloured”), (from δι- (di-, “two”) + χρώς (khrṓs, “colour, complexion”)) + -ic.

senses: The cardinal who administers the Roman Catholic Church in the interregnum between Popes.
ety: Borrowed from Italian camerlengo (“chamberlain”). Doublet of chamberlain.
examples: For the conclave, the camerlengo is now responsible for ensuring an “orderly election and its privacy”, according to Universi Dominici Gregis—the apostolic constitution governing papal succession.

senses: The matrimony vine (Lycium barbarum).
ety: Likely borrowed from Tamil முளரி (muḷari, “bramble”).

senses: The destruction of hair roots by means of an electric current.
ety: Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday. From electro- + -lysis (“a loosening”). Originally of tumors, later (1909) of hair removal.

senses: Producing blood
Spread by blood
ety: From hemato- + -genous.

senses: Someone or something that introduces.
ety: From introduce + -er.

senses: The dried seed of a large evergreen broad-leaved tree, Elaeocarpus ganitrus, which is traditionally used as prayer beads in Hinduism.
ety: From Sanskrit रुद्राक्ष (rudrākṣa, “Rudra's eyes”), from रुद्र (Rudra, “Rudra, a Rigvedic deity of wind and storm”), and अक्ष (ákṣa, “eye”), variant form of अक्षि (ákṣi).
examples: One of my favorite photographs shows a Hindu sadhu right out of central casting – naked body, long matted hair and beard, ash-smeared forehead, rudraksha-mala around his neck, the works – chatting away on a mobile phone.

senses: A form of Japanese verse in which short poems are connected together, the origin of haikai and haiku.
ety: From Japanese 連歌 (renga, literally “connected verse”).

senses: Saiga tatarica, an antelope which inhabits a vast area between Kalmykia, Kazakhstan, southern Siberia.
ety: Russian сайга́ (sajgá, “saiga”), from Kazakh сайғақ (sayğaq, “saiga”), from Proto-Turkic *saygak (“saiga”).

senses: Asian street food consisting of a developing duck embryo boiled alive and eaten in the shell
ety: Borrowed from Malay balut and Tagalog balut.

senses: Of a woman: in a socially imposed state of seclusion or purdah.
ety: Ultimately from Classical Persian گوشه (gōša, “corner”) likely through some Indian language.

senses: The beam of coherent gamma rays produced by such a device.
ety: Acronym of Gamma Ray Amplification by the Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

senses: The process of radicalizing.
ety: From radical + -ization.
examples: From there, it was only a short step to “Kekism,” at once a joke religion and a precursor of the reactionary radicalization to follow.
One way to see the radicalization of the likes of Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, and Megyn Kelly is that they are adopting Fuentes-Lite positions on issues like immigration and vaccines.

senses: The process or action of spilling.
That which has been spilled.
ety: From spill + -age.

senses: A bread-like fermented food made from chopped and grated ensete pulp, a staple of Ethiopian cuisine.
ety: Borrowed from Ge'ez ቆጮ (ḳoč̣o).

senses: Infection by maggots under the skin of cows, or by sheep maggots in the frontal sinus of sheep.
ety: Possibly a modification of Scottish Gaelic boiteag 'maggot'
